code:
spec:
  replicas: 3
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      maxSurge: 1
      maxUnavailable: 0
expl: maxSurge=1 permits the controller to create one extra Pod above the desired count of 3 before removing any old one, capping the total at 4 during the transition. maxUnavailable=0 is the stricter, more interesting constraint here: it means the number of currently-available Pods may never fall below the full desired count of 3, not even briefly -- so the controller cannot delete an old Pod until a new one has already been created AND confirmed Ready, since deleting first would momentarily drop availability to 2. This combination (surge above, zero tolerance for unavailability) is a common choice for latency-sensitive services where even a few seconds of reduced capacity is unacceptable, at the cost of the rollout needing to briefly run one extra Pod's worth of resources at each step.

spec:

  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      maxSurge: 0%
      maxUnavailable: 100%
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: web
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: web
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: nginx
          image: nginx:1.26
expl: With maxSurge: 0% the controller can never create a new Pod before removing an old one (there's no room to surge above the desired count at all), and with maxUnavailable: 100% it's simultaneously permitted to let every single old Pod become unavailable at once. Combined, the only sequence available to the controller is: delete all old Pods first, then create new ones -- which is a full outage, functionally identical to the Recreate strategy, despite being configured as 'RollingUpdate.' The fix inverts the intent correctly: a nonzero maxSurge (25%, matching the default, meaning one extra Pod for a desired count of 4) lets new Pods be created and confirmed Ready before any old ones are removed, and maxUnavailable: 0 forbids the available count from ever dropping below the desired total, which together restore a genuine zero-downtime rollout rather than the 'fast' but outage-causing one that was configured.

So the Endpoints object ends up with exactly 3 addresses (pod-a, pod-b, pod-c), and pod-d -- despite matching the selector -- correctly receives zero traffic from this Service until its readiness probe starts passing.

exp: It still shows the OLD value, "info". Environment variables sourced from a ConfigMap are resolved once, at container start, and baked into that process's environment block -- there is no live mechanism that updates an already-running process's environment. Only a new Pod, created after the ConfigMap change, would show "debug".
code:

kubectl exec web-7d9f8c9b7-4x2lp -- printenv LOG_LEVEL   # ?
expl: envFrom (and configMapKeyRef) resolve their values exactly once, at the moment the container process is started, and the resulting values are written directly into that process's environment block by the container runtime -- there's no ongoing connection back to the ConfigMap object after that point. Updating the ConfigMap changes the object stored in etcd, but it does not reach into any already-running container and rewrite its environment; that's simply not a capability environment variables have. The already-running Pod queried here was started before the update, so printenv correctly reports the stale value, "info", and will continue to do so indefinitely unless that specific Pod is deleted and replaced by a fresh one, which would then resolve envFrom fresh at its own startup and pick up "debug".

git add secret.yaml

expl: The original script's actual bug has nothing to do with 'Secret vs ConfigMap' -- it's that the literal, real password is written into a plain YAML file (secret.yaml) containing nothing more than a base64 encoding of it, and that file is then committed to git, where it becomes permanently recoverable by anyone with repository access via a single base64 -d, and stays recoverable in history even after later deletion. The fix removes both problems at once: DB_PASSWORD is read from an environment variable injected by the CI system's own secret store at deploy time (never hardcoded in the script or committed anywhere), and the rendered manifest is piped directly into kubectl apply -f - rather than ever being written to a file on disk, let alone added to git. The security review's underlying point stands regardless of object kind: the author's 'Secrets are encrypted' defense is itself the misconception this concept warns about -- base64 provides no real confidentiality, so committing a rendered Secret manifest is exactly as dangerous as committing the plaintext value directly.

  --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -

exp: 10. --set sits at the highest precedence level, above any -f file and above the chart's own values.yaml, regardless of the order the flags appear on the command line -- so replicaCount=10 wins over both replicaCount: 3 (values-prod.yaml) and replicaCount: 2 (the chart's default).
code:
helm upgrade web ./my-app \
  -f values-prod.yaml \
  --set replicaCount=10
expl: Helm resolves conflicting values by a fixed precedence order, independent of the order flags are typed: --set (and --set-string/--set-file) always wins over any -f/--values file, which in turn always wins over the chart's own bundled values.yaml. Here, replicaCount is defined three times -- 2 in the chart's default values.yaml, 3 in values-prod.yaml, and 10 via --set -- and since --set is the highest-precedence source, the rendered Deployment ends up with replicas: 10. This is precisely why --set is the standard tool for a temporary, ad hoc override during an incident: it doesn't require editing or committing a change to values-prod.yaml at all, and its effect is scoped to just this one upgrade invocation.

code:

helm upgrade web ./my-app --set image.tag=1.1
helm upgrade web ./my-app --set image.tag=1.2
helm rollback web 1

expl: Before the rollback, the release has three revisions: 1 (tag 1.0), 2 (tag 1.1), 3 (tag 1.2, currently deployed). helm rollback web 1 does not resurrect revision 1 as-is or delete revisions 2 and 3 -- it creates a new revision, 4, whose rendered manifests and values are copied from revision 1's stored state, and marks that new revision 4 as deployed. So the answer has two independent parts: the revision NUMBER that's now current is 4 (the counter only ever climbs), while the actual running CONTENT (image tag 1.0) matches revision 1's, because that's what was rolled back to. A subsequent helm history web would show four entries total: 1, 2, 3 all superseded, and 4 deployed with a description like 'Rollback to 1'.

expl: helm install is a one-time-only operation -- calling it again against a release name that already exists fails outright with exactly the error shown, mirroring how kubectl create behaves against an object that already exists. helm upgrade --install (the --install flag, often abbreviated -i) is designed specifically for this repeated-deploy-from-CI scenario: it upgrades the release if web already exists, or performs a first-time install if it doesn't, so the same command works correctly on the very first deploy and every deploy after it, with no branching logic needed in the script at all. Adding --atomic --timeout 5m on top (not strictly required to fix the reported error, but a meaningful CI/CD safety improvement covered in this concept) also ensures a broken image tag self-heals back to the previous good revision automatically rather than leaving a half-upgraded release in place.

exp: No -- this is not possible with a Service alone, regardless of how it's configured. A Service's spec has only a selector and a list of port mappings; there is no field for a URL path or a hostname anywhere in the Service API. Path-based routing requires inspecting the HTTP request line inside the packet's payload, which is exactly what kube-proxy's Layer 4 packet rewriting never does.
code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: api
spec:
  selector:
    app: api
  ports:
    - port: 80
      targetPort: 8080
expl: The Service API genuinely has no mechanism for this -- it's not a matter of finding the right field, because the field doesn't exist. Every routing decision a Service makes is based purely on the destination IP:port a packet arrives with, rewritten to a backing Pod's IP:targetPort by kube-proxy, entirely without ever parsing what's inside that packet's payload. A URL path like /api/orders lives inside the HTTP request line, which is payload, not addressing information -- so no combination of Service fields, however creative, could make this routing decision, because the layer a Service operates at is structurally one level below where paths and hostnames exist at all. This is exactly the gap Ingress and an Ingress controller are built to fill.

code:
kubectl get svc -A -l tier=frontend -o wide
# NAMESPACE   NAME        TYPE           EXTERNAL-IP    PORT(S)
# team-a      orders      LoadBalancer   203.0.113.21   443:31101/TCP
# team-a      inventory   LoadBalancer   203.0.113.22   443:31102/TCP
# team-b      accounts    LoadBalancer   203.0.113.23   443:31103/TCP
# team-b      billing     LoadBalancer   203.0.113.24   443:31104/TCP
# team-c      search      LoadBalancer   203.0.113.25   443:31105/TCP
# team-c      reports     LoadBalancer   203.0.113.26   443:31106/TCP
# (TLS termination is configured independently, per Service, via each team's own proxy sidecar or cloud LB cert config)
expl: The slowness and error-proneness isn't caused by any misconfiguration in an individual Service -- it's the direct consequence of having six completely independent external entry points, each with its own TLS termination configured separately, owned across three different teams with three different (and possibly inconsistent) processes for actually installing a certificate. Renewing one wildcard cert here means coordinating six separate changes, in six separate places, any one of which can be missed, misconfigured, or delayed relative to the others -- exactly the operational sprawl problem inherent to a one-LoadBalancer-per-app pattern. The structural fix is to consolidate: convert these six Services to plain internal ClusterIP (removing their individual external IPs and LoadBalancer costs entirely), and put a single Ingress controller -- backed by just one LoadBalancer Service -- in front of all of them, with routing rules (covered in the next concept) directing each hostname or path to the right internal Service. From that point on, the wildcard certificate is installed and rotated in exactly one place, regardless of how many internal applications sit behind it.

With no other rule to fall back to, the client would receive a 404 from the Ingress controller itself, not a response from v1-svc.
code:
spec:
  rules:
    - host: api.example.com
      http:
        paths:
          - path: /v1
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service:
                name: v1-svc
                port:

expl: pathType: Prefix splits both the declared path and the incoming request path into segments on '/' and requires the declared segments to match a full, leading run of the request's segments -- it is not a raw string.startswith() comparison. /v1's only segment is 'v1'; the request /v1beta/users has a first segment of 'v1beta', a completely different segment string, not 'v1' with something appended. Because 'v1' != 'v1beta' as whole segments, this rule does not match at all, even though the literal text /v1 is indeed a character-for-character prefix of /v1beta. With no other rule declared to catch this path, the Ingress controller has nothing to route it to and returns its own 404, meaning v1-svc's Pods never see this request and are entirely uninvolved in the failure.

code:
kubectl exec somepod -n frontend -- nslookup api
# Address: ?
expl: DNS resolution for a bare short name is entirely namespace-relative to whichever Pod is doing the lookup, via that Pod's own resolv.conf search list, which always tries the calling Pod's own namespace suffix first. Since frontend genuinely does contain a Service named api, that lookup succeeds on the very first attempt (api.frontend.svc.cluster.local), and the resolver has no reason to try any further suffix, so it never even considers backend's api Service at all. The caller ends up silently talking to the wrong Service, with a perfectly successful, error-free DNS resolution the entire way -- which is exactly why any cross-namespace reference should use at least api.backend (letting the search list fill in the rest) or the fully-qualified name, rather than depending on a bare short name whose meaning is entirely contingent on what else happens to exist in the caller's own namespace.

expl: Resolving web-headless.default.svc.cluster.local (the headless Service's own name, with no Pod prefix) returns an A record for every currently-Ready backing Pod -- web-0, web-1, and web-2's IPs all at once -- and which one a given DNS client or connection library actually chooses to use first is effectively arbitrary from the application's perspective, which is exactly the inconsistency being observed. The fix is to use the per-Pod DNS name specifically, prefixing the individual Pod's own name onto the headless Service's name: web-0.web-headless.default.svc.cluster.local resolves to exactly one address -- web-0's own IP, and only web-0's -- regardless of how many other replicas exist or what state they're in. This is precisely the mechanism StatefulSets pair with headless Services to enable in the first place: addressing one specific, named replica deterministically, rather than an unordered pool.

code: kubectl logs app-pod-xyz
expl: This error specifically means the target Pod has multiple containers (likely a main app container plus a sidecar, such as a log shipper), and kubectl logs refuses to guess which one you meant -- unlike a single-container Pod, where it has an unambiguous default. The fix is to first list the Pod's container names (via kubectl get pod ... -o jsonpath, or kubectl describe pod) and then supply -c <container-name> to kubectl logs to specify exactly which container's stream to read. This is precisely the multi-container-Pod detail introduced back in the Pods concept -- a Pod's containers are independent processes with independent log streams, and nothing about being in the same Pod merges them into one.

exp: The Pod is considered Ready as soon as its container is Running (the default with no readinessProbe), so the Service adds it to Endpoints and starts routing real traffic to it immediately -- including during the 20-second window before its database connection is actually ready, during which any request it receives will error.
code:
containers:
  - name: app
    image: my-app:1.0
    livenessProbe:
      httpGet:
        path: /healthz
        port: 8080
      initialDelaySeconds: 5
    # no readinessProbe defined
expl: Without a readinessProbe, Kubernetes has no configured way to know that this application needs roughly 20 seconds after starting before it can genuinely handle requests -- the only thing being checked is liveness, and even that doesn't start until initialDelaySeconds: 5 has elapsed, and it's checking a completely different thing (process responsiveness) than 'is the DB connection ready.' With no readiness signal defined at all, the Pod's Ready condition defaults to true the moment its container reaches Running, so it's added to the Service's Endpoints immediately and starts receiving real traffic well before the 20-second warm-up finishes, producing exactly the class of request errors this concept describes. The fix is adding a readinessProbe (an httpGet against a /ready endpoint the app only reports healthy on once its DB connection is actually established, for example) so the Pod is correctly excluded from traffic during that specific window.

code:
livenessProbe:
  httpGet:
    path: /healthz
    port: 8080
  periodSeconds: 5
  timeoutSeconds: 1
  failureThreshold: 1
expl: Clean application logs with no crash, paired with restarts that clearly correspond to Killing/Unhealthy events in kubectl describe pod, points squarely at the liveness probe itself as the thing destroying otherwise-healthy containers -- and timeoutSeconds: 1 with failureThreshold: 1 means a single HTTP response taking just over one second, which is exactly the kind of transient slowdown moderate load can easily cause, is enough on its own to count as a liveness failure and trigger an immediate kill-and-restart. Raising timeoutSeconds to 3 gives each individual check meaningfully more headroom before it's even counted as failed, and raising failureThreshold to 3 additionally requires three consecutive failures (roughly 15 seconds of sustained unresponsiveness at periodSeconds: 5) before a restart is triggered, rather than one isolated slow tick -- converting the probe from something that reacts to normal load variance into something that only reacts to a genuinely sustained hang, which is what a liveness probe should be checking for in the first place.

# web-abc123  500m         310Mi

# Application-level symptom: request latency has crept up 4x under moderate load,
# with no errors and no crashes anywhere in kubectl logs.

# defaultRequest: { cpu: 100m, memory: 128Mi }
# default:        { cpu: 500m, memory: 512Mi }

# A developer submits this Pod spec with NO resources block at all:

metadata:
  name: forgot-resources
spec:
  containers:
    - name: app
      image: my-app:1.0

# What actually gets scheduled and run (after the LimitRange's defaults are applied):
# containers:
#   - name: app
#     resources:
#       requests: { cpu: 100m, memory: 128Mi }
#       limits:   { cpu: 500m, memory: 512Mi }

exp: The container is killed by the kernel's OOM killer the moment its actual usage tries to exceed the 256Mi limit -- the 128Mi request is irrelevant at this point, since it only mattered for scheduling. kubectl describe pod would show Last State: Terminated, Reason: OOMKilled, Exit Code: 137, and the kubelet would then restart the container per its restartPolicy, incrementing RESTARTS.
code:
resources:
  requests:
    memory: 128Mi
  limits:
    memory: 256Mi
expl: The 128Mi request was consumed entirely at scheduling time -- it played no role in this container's actual runtime behavior once it was placed on a node. What matters now is the 256Mi limit, enforced continuously by the kernel via the container's cgroup: memory is an incompressible resource, so there's no way for the kernel to force the process to simply use less RAM in the moment it tries to allocate past the limit. Instead, the OOM killer intervenes and sends SIGKILL, terminating the process outright. kubectl describe pod would report this precisely as Reason: OOMKilled with Exit Code: 137 (128 + signal 9), and depending on the Pod's restartPolicy (Always, by default, for Pods managed by a Deployment), the kubelet restarts the container afterward, which is what causes the RESTARTS count to climb -- and if the process's real memory needs genuinely exceed 256Mi under normal operation rather than as a one-off spike, this same OOMKilled cycle will very likely repeat indefinitely until the limit itself is raised or the application's memory usage is reduced.

code:
resources:
  requests:
    cpu: 100m
    memory: 256Mi
  limits:
    cpu: 100m
    memory: 512Mi
expl: With cpu limits set to exactly 100m (one-tenth of a single core) and no crashes or restarts anywhere in the picture, this is a textbook CPU throttling symptom, not a memory or crash-related one: the container is being denied additional CPU time by the kernel's CFS bandwidth controller every time it exhausts its very small 100m-per-period quota, which manifests purely as slowness -- exactly the 4x latency increase reported -- with zero visibility in RESTARTS, Terminated reasons, or logs, since nothing about the process itself is failing. Raising the cpu limit substantially (to 1000m, a full core, here) gives the container real headroom to use more CPU time under load before hitting its ceiling and being throttled again, and raising cpu requests alongside it (to 500m) ensures the scheduler actually reserves enough CPU capacity on whichever node this Pod lands on to support that higher limit being used in practice, rather than relying on unreserved, potentially contended capacity to make the higher limit meaningful.

code:
resources:
  requests:
    cpu: 500m
    memory: 256Mi
  limits:
    cpu: 1000m
    memory: 512Mi

# NAME     STATUS    NODE

# cat: /var/lib/db-data/data.log: No such file or directory

exp: The file survives the container restart (still prints 'v1') because emptyDir belongs to the Pod, not the individual container. It disappears at the second point -- after `kubectl delete pod` -- because deleting the Pod removes its emptyDir directory from the node entirely, and the replacement Pod (a new, unrelated object) gets a brand-new, empty emptyDir with no connection to the deleted one.
code:
kubectl exec cache-pod -- sh -c 'echo v1 > /cache/data.txt'
# container crashes, kubelet restarts it in place
kubectl exec cache-pod -- cat /cache/data.txt   # ?

kubectl delete pod cache-pod
# ReplicaSet creates a new Pod, cache-pod-7f2ab
kubectl exec cache-pod-7f2ab -- cat /cache/data.txt   # ?
expl: The container crash-and-restart is a Pod-internal event: the kubelet replaces the container process but the Pod object, and therefore its emptyDir volume, is untouched, so the first `cat` still prints 'v1'. Deleting the Pod is categorically different -- the Pod object is gone, and the kubelet cleans up the emptyDir directory it was backing on that node. The ReplicaSet's replacement Pod, `cache-pod-7f2ab`, is a new object built from the same template, but Kubernetes makes no attempt to carry forward the old Pod's emptyDir contents -- there's no mechanism that even could, since emptyDir has no identity independent of the specific Pod it was created for. The second `cat` therefore fails with 'No such file or directory'.

code:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: kv-cache
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: kv-cache
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: kv-cache
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: kv-cache
          image: kv-cache:2.0
          volumeMounts:
            - name: data
              mountPath: /data
      volumes:
        - name: data
          hostPath:
            path: /var/lib/kv-cache-data
            type: DirectoryOrCreate
expl: The bug is architectural, not syntactic: hostPath ties `/data` to whichever node's local disk the Pod happened to be running on at the time -- node maintenance forcing a reschedule onto a different node is exactly the scenario hostPath cannot survive, because the new node's `/var/lib/kv-cache-data` has never been written to. The real fix is to stop coupling the Pod's storage to a specific node at all, by requesting storage through a PersistentVolumeClaim instead (`claimName: kv-cache-data`, referencing a PVC backed by network-attached storage such as a cloud block volume). That storage exists as its own resource, independent of any node, and can be attached to whichever node the rescheduled Pod actually lands on -- exactly the property hostPath structurally cannot offer, and exactly what the PersistentVolumes and PersistentVolumeClaims concept covers next.

exp: It stays Pending indefinitely -- it will not resolve on its own, no matter how long you wait. EBS-backed storage is fundamentally block storage that only supports single-node attachment, so the ebs-gp3 provisioner has no way to ever satisfy a ReadWriteMany request; this isn't a slow provisioning operation, it's a structurally unsatisfiable one.

metadata:

spec:

  resources:

expl: Unlike a normal provisioning delay (typically resolved within seconds), this PVC requests an access mode that the only available StorageClass's underlying technology cannot provide under any circumstances -- AWS EBS volumes attach to exactly one node at a time, by design, at the infrastructure level, regardless of what Kubernetes asks for. The binding/provisioning controller will keep trying and keep failing, surfacing a ProvisioningFailed event via kubectl describe pvc, but there is no amount of waiting that fixes this -- the actual fix requires either changing the access mode to ReadWriteOnce (if single-node access is actually sufficient) or provisioning against a genuinely different StorageClass backed by a real network filesystem (NFS, EFS, CephFS) that can honor ReadWriteMany.

StorageClass name references are exact-string matches with no case normalization, exactly like Service label selectors, so `Fast-SSD` simply doesn't refer to anything that exists, and the PVC can never bind or provision against a StorageClass that isn't there. Correcting the case to match the real object name (`fast-ssd`) lets the provisioner pick up the PVC normally, and it should move to Bound within seconds.

exp: Scale-down deletes cache-2 first, then cache-1, leaving cache-0. Scale-up recreates cache-1 first, then cache-2, each waited on to become Ready before the next starts. Their volumes come back with their PREVIOUS data intact -- by default, scaling down does not delete the PVCs for the removed ordinals, so scaling back up reattaches cache-1 and cache-2 to the same data-cache-1 and data-cache-2 PVCs they had before.

# deletion order: ?

kubectl scale statefulset cache --replicas=3
# creation order: ?
# cache-1 and cache-2's volumes: fresh, or previous data?
expl: StatefulSet scale-down always proceeds in strictly descending ordinal order -- the highest-numbered Pod is removed first -- so cache-2 goes before cache-1, leaving cache-0 as the sole survivor. Scaling back up to 3 proceeds in strictly ascending order, and under the default OrderedReady policy, cache-1 must be Running and Ready before cache-2 is even created. Critically, the PVCs created by volumeClaimTemplates for the now-removed ordinals are not deleted by a scale-down by default -- they're simply left bound but unused, still holding their data -- so when cache-1 and cache-2 are recreated on scale-up, the StatefulSet controller reattaches each to its own pre-existing PVC (data-cache-1, data-cache-2 respectively), and both come back with exactly the data they had before, not a fresh empty volume.

code:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: cache
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: cache
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: cache
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: cache
          image: cache-node:1.0
          volumeMounts:
            - name: data
              mountPath: /data
      volumes:
        - name: data
          persistentVolumeClaim:
            claimName: cache-data
expl: The original Deployment gives every one of its 3 replicas the exact same, single claimName: cache-data -- there is only ever one PVC involved, no matter how many replicas exist, because a Deployment's Pod template has no concept of a per-replica claim. Since that PVC is ReadWriteOnce, it can only be mounted read-write on one node at a time; any replica scheduled to a different node than whichever one already has it attached gets stuck Pending with a volume node affinity conflict, and any replicas that do happen to share a node are all reading and writing the identical shared volume, not independent data. Converting to a StatefulSet with volumeClaimTemplates fixes this at the root: Kubernetes now generates one distinct PVC per ordinal (data-cache-0, data-cache-1, data-cache-2), so each replica gets its own dedicated 5Gi volume, can be scheduled to any node without conflicting with the others, and keeps that same specific volume across any future replacement of that ordinal.

code:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet
metadata:
  name: cache
spec:
  serviceName: cache
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: cache
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: cache
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: cache
          image: cache-node:1.0
          volumeMounts:
            - name: data
              mountPath: /data
  volumeClaimTemplates:
    - metadata:
        name: data
      spec:
        accessModes: ["ReadWriteOnce"]
        resources:
          requests:
            storage: 5Gi

kubectl create deployment web --image=nginx:1.25
kubectl scale deployment web --replicas=3
kubectl set image deployment/web nginx=nginx:1.26

# web-deployment.yaml declares: this Deployment should have 3 replicas of nginx:1.26
kubectl apply -f web-deployment.yaml

# Running it again with the SAME file is a no-op -- nothing changes, no error
kubectl apply -f web-deployment.yaml

# Compare: running the imperative 'create' twice fails outright
kubectl create deployment web --image=nginx:1.26
kubectl create deployment web --image=nginx:1.26
# Error from server (AlreadyExists): deployments.apps "web" already exists

# Someone manually bumps replicas to 5 directly on the live object
kubectl edit deployment web
# ... they type replicas: 5 and save; kubectl confirms 'deployment.apps/web edited'

kubectl get deployment web -o jsonpath='{.spec.replicas}'
# 5

# An hour later, an automated pipeline reapplies the ORIGINAL, unmodified file (still replicas: 3)
kubectl apply -f web-deployment.yaml

kubectl get deployment web -o jsonpath='{.spec.replicas}'
# 3  -- the manual bump to 5 is gone, with no warning

exp: Right after the scale command, the count is 5. After the second apply, the count drops back to 2 -- the file was never updated to reflect the scale, so apply treats 2 as the declared truth and corrects the drift.
code:
kubectl apply -f web-deployment.yaml   # file says replicas: 2
kubectl scale deployment web --replicas=5
kubectl get deployment web -o jsonpath='{.spec.replicas}'   # ?

# ...an hour later...
kubectl apply -f web-deployment.yaml   # SAME file, still says replicas: 2
kubectl get deployment web -o jsonpath='{.spec.replicas}'   # ?
expl: kubectl scale is an imperative action: it patches spec.replicas on the live object directly, giving an immediate count of 5, but it never touches web-deployment.yaml or the last-applied-configuration annotation that apply consults. An hour later, when the unmodified file (still declaring replicas: 2) is reapplied, apply computes what needs to change to match the file's declared state -- and since the file has always said 2, apply patches the live object back down to 2, silently erasing the manual scale. This is the same drift-correction behavior as a manual kubectl edit being overwritten: whatever isn't captured in the file the automation applies gets treated as something to correct, not something to preserve.

kubectl create has no diffing or reconciliation logic at all -- it issues a single 'insert this object' request, and if an object with that name already exists, the API server correctly rejects it with AlreadyExists, because create was never designed to handle 'this might already exist and that's fine.' kubectl apply, by contrast, is explicitly designed for exactly this repeated-invocation scenario: it computes what (if anything) needs to change between the live object and the file, and issues a patch instead of an insert when the object already exists, making it a true no-op on repeated runs with an unchanged file. Swapping create for apply is precisely why teams standardize on apply for anything driven by a CI pipeline or GitOps controller.

exp: 'Scheduled' always appears first. The kubelet (which emits 'Started' once it actually starts the container) only ever watches for Pods that already have a nodeName assigned to its own node -- it has nothing to act on until the scheduler has written that binding, so Scheduled is a hard prerequisite, not just a usual convention.
code:
kubectl apply -f web-deployment.yaml
kubectl get events -w
expl: 'Scheduled' is emitted by the scheduler the moment it writes a nodeName binding onto the Pod object. 'Started' is emitted much later by the kubelet on that specific node, after it has watched for Pods bound to itself, pulled the image via the container runtime, and actually started the container process. There is no orchestrator forcing this order as a policy -- it's a structural data dependency: the kubelet's watch is filtered to Pods already assigned to its node, so a kubelet literally has nothing to react to until a nodeName exists. No amount of speed or luck lets Started happen before Scheduled, because the event the kubelet reacts to (a Pod bound to its node) doesn't exist yet until the scheduler creates it.

code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: web-abc123
spec:
  containers:
    - name: nginx
      image: nginx:1.26
      resources:
        requests:
          cpu: "16"
          memory: "256Mi"
expl: The Pod requested 16 full CPU cores (cpu: "16"), but every node in the cluster only has 4 CPUs total -- so no single node, even completely idle, could ever satisfy that request, which is exactly what '0/3 nodes are available: 3 Insufficient cpu' is reporting. This is a scheduler-stage failure specifically: the scheduler's job is to find a node with enough unallocated capacity to cover every resource request on the Pod, and it correctly refuses to schedule the Pod anywhere rather than overcommit a node beyond its capacity. The fix reduces the request to something realistic for an nginx container -- 250m (250 millicpu, a quarter of one core) -- which comfortably fits on any of the 4-CPU nodes. The broader lesson: resources.requests should reflect what the container actually needs on an ongoing basis, not an arbitrarily large number 'just to be safe' -- oversized requests are a common, very real cause of Pods that silently never schedule at all.

exp: Kubernetes accepts the manifest -- there's no validation against duplicate containerPort declarations. But at runtime, whichever container's process tries to bind port 8080 second will fail with an 'address already in use' error, because both containers share exactly one network namespace and therefore one port space for the whole Pod. That container will likely crash-loop. Two separate Pods each binding 8080 would have no conflict at all, because each Pod gets its own independent network namespace and IP.
code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: port-conflict
spec:
  containers:
    - name: server-a
      image: my-server:1.0
      ports:
        - containerPort: 8080
    - name: server-b
      image: my-other-server:1.0
      ports:
        - containerPort: 8080
expl: containerPort in a Pod spec is documentation/metadata for humans and tooling -- it doesn't reserve the port or prevent a collision; Kubernetes does not validate that two containers in the same Pod use different ports. The actual conflict happens at the OS level, inside whichever container's process calls bind(8080) second within that shared network namespace, and fails exactly the way two ordinary processes on one host would if both tried to listen on the same port. Depending on restartPolicy, the kubelet will likely keep restarting the failing container, producing a CrashLoopBackOff. This has nothing to do with containers in isolation -- two entirely separate Pods, each with its own independent network namespace and IP, could both happily bind port 8080 with zero conflict, because 'the port space' is scoped per-Pod, not global to the node or the cluster.

code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: app
spec:
  containers:
    - name: wait-for-db
      image: busybox:1.36
      command: ["sh", "-c", "until nc -z db 5432; do sleep 1; done"]
    - name: app
      image: my-app:1.0
expl: In the original spec, wait-for-db was listed under `containers`, which means it starts at roughly the same time as app, with no guarantee it finishes -- or even starts -- before app tries to connect to the database, which is exactly the race condition described. Moving it into `initContainers` changes its behavior entirely: init containers run to completion, strictly in the order listed, and the kubelet will not start any regular container until every init container has exited successfully (exit code 0). With this fix, `app` is now guaranteed not to start until `wait-for-db`'s loop has actually detected the database is reachable and exited, eliminating the race by construction rather than by hoping the timing works out.

code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: app
spec:
  initContainers:
    - name: wait-for-db
      image: busybox:1.36
      command: ["sh", "-c", "until nc -z db 5432; do sleep 1; done"]
  containers:
    - name: app
      image: my-app:1.0
